heading: Getting started
text: Sinhron is a private messenger you can run on your own server. This page explains what it is, how to get the app, and what happens the first time you open it, including the one thing you must not skip: writing down your 24-word key. Sinhron is in early beta. There are no App Store or Google Play builds yet, no public releases yet, and the code has not had an independent security audit. Please treat it as a preview, not as a replacement for the messenger you rely on today.

heading: What is Sinhron
text: Sinhron is a messenger for chats, groups, voice and video calls, photos, files and voice messages. Everything you send is end-to-end encrypted: it is locked on your phone and can only be unlocked on the phones of the people you are talking to. The second idea is self-hosting. Sinhron does not run one big central service. Instead, a server is run by someone you trust: you, your family, your company or a friend. The server passes encrypted messages along, but it cannot read them. In the app's own words: "Premium chat. Private by default."

heading: What makes it different
text: No email, no phone, no password. You do not sign up with a phone number or an email address. Your account is a cryptographic key that lives on your device, and a 24-word key lets you restore it. Encryption is always on. There is no unencrypted mode, not for convenience and not for admins. Every chat, group and call is end-to-end encrypted from the very first message. A server you choose. Sinhron runs on a server you trust. Your data lives there and nowhere else: not with us, not with anyone. Setting one up takes a few Docker commands. Built on open standards. Messages use MLS, the IETF standard for group encryption (RFC 9420). Calls use SFrame (RFC 9605). We did not invent our own cryptography. No telemetry. The app does not send analytics or usage data to the developers. Ever. Made to feel good. Smooth animations, careful typography, haptics, dark mode, accessibility. Privacy should not feel like a compromise.

heading: Installing the app
text: When builds are ready, they will be published on GitHub Releases: github.com/Grossmanban/sinhron-website/releases Sinhron is built with Flutter, so one codebase can target iOS, Android, macOS, Windows and Linux. Right now development and testing focus on iPhone. Builds for the other platforms are planned and will appear on the releases page as they become ready. There are no published builds yet. If you are comfortable building from source, the code is at github.com/grossmanban/sinhron. Store versions (App Store, Google Play) will come later and require code signing, which is part of the roadmap.

heading: First launch
text: The first launch takes a couple of minutes. Here is what to expect. Welcome. Three short screens explain the basics: encrypted by default, no email or phone number, and the server you trust. Pick a server. Enter the address of your Sinhron server, for example your-server.com. If you got an invite link, it fills in the details for you. Sinhron works with any server you trust: your team's, a friend's, or your own. The server never sees what you send. Create your profile. Choose the name people will see. Your name is shared inside your encrypted chats, not stored as plain text on the server. Write down your 24-word key. The app shows 24 words. Write them on paper, in order. Quick check. To make sure the words really are on paper, the app asks you for three of them by number, each with four options. If you pick the wrong one, it tells you which word to look at again, and you can go back to the list. Setting up. The app creates your keys and connects to the server. You are ready to chat. To start a conversation, open New chat and either scan your contact's QR code or paste their key (64 characters). There is no phone book to search, because there are no phone numbers.

heading: Your 24-word key
text: Your 24 words are your account. They are generated on your phone using the BIP-39 standard, and all of your keys are derived from them. It is the only way to restore your account. If you lose your phone or reinstall the app, choose "Restore with your key" and type the 24 words. Sinhron recovers your identity and your membership in your chats and groups from an encrypted backup that only your key can open. Please keep in mind: Store it offline. Paper in a safe place is best. Do not keep it in a screenshot, a notes app, an email draft or a chat. Nobody can recover it for you. The words never leave your device and are never sent to the server. We cannot reset them, and neither can your server's admin. A lost key means a lost account. Without the 24 words, the encrypted backup cannot be opened by anyone. You would need to create a new account. Anyone with the words can become you. Treat them like the keys to your home. Restoring with your key brings back your identity and your chats and groups. It does not bring back your old message history: that is stored only on your devices, encrypted, and is not uploaded anywhere. If another of your devices is still signed in, it passes the recent

heading: What's next
text: Features: everything you can do in Sinhron, from reactions to disappearing messages. Security: how encryption works and what the server can and cannot see. Threat model: what Sinhron protects against, and what it does not. Self-hosting: run your own Sinhron server. FAQ: short answers to common questions.

heading: Features
text: Sinhron aims to feel like a premium messenger while keeping everything end-to-end encrypted. This page walks through what you can do today. Where something is still in beta or not built yet, we say so.

heading: Chats and groups
text: You can have one-on-one chats and group chats. Every chat, including a one-on-one chat, is an encrypted MLS group under the hood, so the same protection applies everywhere. To start a chat, open New chat and scan your contact's QR code or paste their key. There are no phone numbers and no public directory, so people can only reach you if you share your code or key with them. In groups, everyone shares their own display name with the chat, inside the encryption; the server never learns it. The name appears above that person's messages. Until someone has shared a name, a short form of their key is shown. A name is only a claim, so two people can pick the same one: the safety number is what tells them apart. You can also set a profile photo: in Settings, tap your profile at the top. It travels the same way as your name, inside the encryption, and only to chats you're actually talking in, never to message requests or people you've blocked. Your phone re-encodes the photo first, removing location and camera details, and the other phone re-encodes it again before showing it. It appears in the chat list, the chat header and Chat info. In a group, type @ to mention someone: you pick from t

heading: Messages
text: Press and hold any message to open a menu inspired by iMessage. The message lifts above the blurred chat, with a row of reactions on top and actions below: Reply, Copy, Forward, Pin, Edit, Select and Delete. Reply. Swipe a message to the side, or choose Reply. The quote appears in your message; tap it to jump back to the original. Reactions. Double-tap a text message to send a heart, or pick any reaction from the menu. Tap a reaction chip to add or remove yours. Edit. Fix a typo in your own message within 24 hours of sending it. Edited messages are labelled "edited". Delete. Delete a message just for you, or for everyone (your own messages, within 24 hours). A deleted message really is erased: its text, any media keys, the quote and reactions. After 24 hours, nobody's app accepts an edit or delete of the message, so old history can't be rewritten. Pin. Pin a message to a bar under the chat header, for everyone in the chat. Tap the bar to jump to the message. Select and forward. Select several messages to copy, delete or forward them. Forwarded photos and files are re-encrypted under a new key, so the server cannot link the two chats. Status ticks. Sending, sent, delivered and read.

heading: Photos, video, files and voice
text: Media features are implemented and covered by tests, but have not yet been verified end to end on a real device. Expect rough edges. Every attachment is encrypted on your phone with a fresh key before it is uploaded. The server stores only scrambled bytes; the key travels inside your encrypted message. Photos. Send from the camera or your library, up to 10 at once, with a caption. Several photos arrive together as an album. Before sending, each photo is re-encoded on your device, which strips location (GPS) and other hidden metadata. Gallery. Tap a photo to open it full screen. Swipe through every photo in the chat, pinch or double-tap to zoom, swipe down to close. You can share a photo or save it to your library. Video. Record a video with the camera (up to 3 minutes) or send one from your library. Large clips are compressed to 720p on your phone before they're encrypted, and a still frame travels with the video (encrypted, like a photo thumbnail) so the chat shows a preview. Playback happens from memory, so the decrypted video is never written to disk. Files. Send documents of any type. Open or share them with other apps; the temporary copy is deleted as soon as you are done. Voi

heading: Calls
text: Sinhron supports audio and video calls. Calls are end-to-end encrypted with SFrame (RFC 9605), using keys derived from your chat's MLS encryption. The call server forwards the media but cannot see or hear it. Calls can get through restrictive networks that only allow ordinary HTTPS traffic. If you'd rather not be called, turn off Incoming calls in Privacy: every call is then declined without ringing. Current limitations: Group calls are in beta. They are built, but have not yet been tested on real devices. Incoming calls only ring while the app is open. Ringing on a locked or closed phone requires Apple's push service, which needs an Apple developer certificate that is not set up yet. Calls across different networks on a real deployed server have not been fully tested yet.

heading: Disappearing messages
text: You can make messages in a chat disappear after a set time. Open Chat info (tap the chat's name at the top) and choose Off, 5 minutes, 1 hour, 1 day, 1 week or 4 weeks. Both people see a note when the timer changes, the header shows the current timer, and disappearing messages carry a small timer icon. When the time is up, the message is deleted from both phones completely: the text, photos, video, voice messages and documents, along with their encryption keys. A few things to know: The timer starts when a message is sent (for you) or when it arrives on the other phone, not when it is read. The server can't read disappearing messages, but it does know a chat's timer: it uses it to delete that chat's stored encrypted messages early. Disappearing messages protect against leaks later on. They cannot stop the other person from taking a screenshot. On iPhone, if someone takes a screenshot while a chat with disappearing messages is open, everyone in the chat sees a note about it. The same goes for recording or mirroring the screen: the chat notes it once per recording. A modified app or a second phone's camera won't trigger it, so treat it as a courtesy, not protection.

heading: Folders and archive
text: Organise your chats into folders. Built-in folders are All, Personal, Groups and Unread. You can also create your own: include all personal chats, all groups, or specific chats, and hide muted or read chats. Swipe left and right to move between folders. Each folder tab shows an unread count. Press and hold a folder tab to edit, reorder (drag them), mark all as read, or delete it. Archive chats you want out of the way. Archived chats live in their own screen and do not appear in any folder. In a long list, the Archive row waits above your first chat: pull down to reveal it. A new message brings an archived chat back to the list, unless the chat is muted. Muted chats stay archived. Swipe actions on a chat row: mute or unmute, archive or unarchive, and delete (always with a confirmation).

heading: App lock and privacy
text: App lock. Require Face ID, Touch ID or your device passcode to open Sinhron. Choose when it locks: immediately, or after 1, 5 or 60 minutes in the background. Hide in app switcher. When Sinhron is in the background, a blurred cover with the logo hides your chats from the app switcher. On by default. Read receipts and typing indicators can be turned off. Like in Signal, they are mutual: if you turn them off, you neither send nor see them. Online status is never shown. Link previews are off unless you turn them on. Incoming calls can be switched off entirely. Proxy (Tor). Route all traffic to the server through a SOCKS5 proxy such as Orbot, so the server doesn't see your IP address. Calls don't go through the proxy.

heading: Message requests and blocking
text: When someone you haven't talked to starts a chat with you, it arrives as a message request. Until you accept, they don't see that you've read their messages, don't see you typing, don't learn your name, and their calls don't ring. Instead of the message field you see Accept, Block and Delete. Writing in the chat accepts it too. Block someone from a chat's info screen, or from their row in a group's member list. Their messages, reactions and other actions are dropped on your phone before you ever see them, and calls from them in your personal chat are declined without ringing. You can review and unblock people under Privacy → Blocked. Blocking stays on your device, so the server never learns who you've blocked. In a group, a blocked person is still a member: they can still read what you write there, you just don't see them. All of these live on one Privacy screen, and every switch on it does exactly what it says.

heading: Verifying contacts
text: To be sure you are talking to the right person, and that nobody is in the middle, compare safety numbers. Each chat has a 60-digit number (12 groups of 5 digits) computed from both of your keys. It is the same on both phones. Compare it in person or over a channel you trust. Or tap Scan their code and point the camera at the QR code on their screen: if the codes match, the contact is marked as verified right away, and if they don't, you get a warning. You can also tap Mark as verified yourself, and a checkmark appears next to their name. If your contact's key ever changes, Sinhron shows "Safety number changed" and removes the checkmark, so you can verify again. In groups, every member has their own safety number. Open Chat info and tap a member to check theirs.

heading: Appearance and accessibility
text: Themes: System, Light, Dark and Black (OLED). Six accent colours, adjusted in dark mode for contrast. Chat wallpapers: soft gradients, subtle patterns, or your own photo (kept only on your device). Languages: English and Russian. Sinhron follows your phone's language, or you can choose one in Settings → Appearance → Language. VoiceOver: buttons, tabs, chat rows and messages have spoken labels, and message actions are available from VoiceOver. Larger text: key screens are tested with Dynamic Type at 1.5× and 2× size. Contrast: text and accent colours meet WCAG AA contrast in light and dark themes. Reduce Motion is respected: slides become cross-fades and springy effects are turned off. Sounds and haptics: quiet send and receive sounds and subtle vibrations, each with its own switch.

heading: How security works
text: Sinhron is designed around one assumption: the server should not have to be trusted. This page explains, in plain language first, how your messages, calls and files are protected, and exactly what a server operator can and cannot see. Sinhron has not yet had an independent security audit. The design uses well-studied open standards, but the implementation is young. See Threat model for known limitations.

heading: In short
text: Everything you send is end-to-end encrypted on your device. There is no way to turn it off. The server stores and forwards only encrypted data. Even someone with full access to the server and its database cannot read your messages or see your photos. The server still sees some metadata, such as who is in which chat, when messages arrive and roughly how big they are. We are honest about this below. Your account is a key on your device, backed up by 24 words that never leave your hands. Your local data is encrypted on the device, and you can lock the app with Face ID or Touch ID. Sinhron sends no telemetry to anyone.

heading: Encryption is always on
text: Sinhron has no plain-text mode, not "for convenience", not "for debugging", not "for admins". Every chat is encrypted from its very first message, including one-on-one chats, groups, calls, photos, files, voice messages, reactions, edits and read receipts. Features that cannot work without reading your data on the server, such as server-side search, simply do not exist on the server. Search runs on your device instead.

heading: The MLS protocol
text: Messages are encrypted with MLS (Messaging Layer Security), an open IETF standard published as RFC 9420 in 2023. MLS was designed by cryptographers from across the industry specifically for secure group messaging. Sinhron uses OpenMLS, an open-source implementation written in Rust. We do not use home-made cryptography. What MLS gives you, in plain terms: Only members can read. Every chat is an MLS group. Only the devices in the group hold the keys. Fresh keys over time. The group regularly moves to new keys. Each step is called an epoch. Forward secrecy. If a key is stolen today, older messages stay protected. Post-compromise security. If a device was compromised, the group heals once keys are refreshed: the attacker is locked out of future messages. Changes in membership. When someone is removed from a group, the keys change and they cannot read anything sent afterwards. Authenticated senders. Every message is signed. The server cannot forge a message or pretend to be someone else, and nobody can edit or delete another person's messages. To make message lengths harder to guess, encrypted messages are padded to multiples of 512 bytes, so the server sees a size bucket, not the exact

heading: What the server sees
text: A Sinhron server has to route messages, so it inevitably learns some information about delivery. Here is the honest picture. The server can see The server cannot see --- --- That an account (a public key) exists, and which devices it has Your 24-word key or any private key Which devices are in which chat, so it can deliver ordinary messages and let members into calls The content of any message When messages are sent and delivered, and whom a sealed envelope is for Which chat a sealed message belongs to Approximate message sizes (in 512-byte buckets) Which account sent a sealed message, once access keys have been shared Approximate sizes of encrypted attachments, and when they are uploaded and downloaded Your name, chat names or group names Your IP address when you connect, unless you use a proxy such as Tor Photos, videos, files and voice messages, their names and types Each chat's disappearing-messages timer, so it can delete stored copies on time Whether a message is text, a reaction, an edit or a receipt The size and update frequency of your encrypted backup What is inside your backup That a call is taking place and who joined it What is said or shown in a call Whom you have blo

heading: Calls and SFrame
text: Calls go through LiveKit, an open-source media server that Sinhron runs alongside the main server. LiveKit is an SFU (selective forwarding unit): it forwards each participant's audio and video to the others without mixing them. On top of the normal connection encryption, every audio and video frame is encrypted end to end with SFrame, a standard published as RFC 9605. The SFrame keys are derived from the MLS keys of your chat, exactly as RFC 9605 describes. That means: The keys are created only on the participants' devices and are never sent to any server. LiveKit forwards encrypted frames it cannot decrypt. When the chat's keys change, the call's keys change too. Call keys live only in memory during the call. They are never written to disk or logged. Only members of the chat can get a ticket to join its call. A relay server (coturn) helps calls get through firewalls and NAT; it only ever sees encrypted traffic, and its logins do not reveal who is calling. LiveKit does see which accounts joined a call, when, and from which IP addresses, and it sees packet sizes and timing.

heading: Data on your device
text: Your chats are stored in a local database that is fully encrypted with SQLCipher, a widely used encrypted version of SQLite (AES-256). The encryption key is derived from your 24-word key. Decrypted photos and videos stay in memory. They are not saved to disk. When the system requires a file, for example to share a document or record a voice message, Sinhron uses a short-lived temporary file and deletes it right away. Protected files and keys. On iOS, the app's files are also protected by the system until the phone is first unlocked after a restart. The key that opens your database is kept in the iOS Keychain, on this device only, so Sinhron reopens without asking for your 24 words, and your phone's passcode and app lock are what protect it. Photos lose their metadata. Before sending, each photo is re-encoded on your device, so location data and other hidden metadata never leave your phone. App lock. You can require Face ID, Touch ID or your device passcode to open Sinhron, immediately or after a few minutes in the background. App switcher cover. When Sinhron is in the background, a blurred cover hides your chats from the app switcher.

heading: Backup and your 24-word key
text: When you create an account, your phone generates a 24-word key using the BIP-39 standard. All of your account keys are derived from it. So that you can get back into your chats on a new phone, Sinhron keeps an encrypted backup of your encryption state (your membership in chats and groups) on your server. The backup is encrypted on your device with a key derived from your 24 words, using AES-256-GCM. The server stores it but cannot open it; it only sees its size, how often it changes, and a version counter. The 24 words are shown once, are never sent to the server and are never logged. The backup restores your identity and your chats and groups. It does not contain your message history. If you lose the 24 words, the backup cannot be opened by anyone, including you, us, or the server's operator. This is a deliberate choice: it is better to lose access than to hand a recovery key to a server.

heading: Notifications without content
text: Push notifications travel through Apple's and Google's servers, so Sinhron never puts anything meaningful in them. A notification carries no message text, no sender and no chat identifier, only an unread count and a generic "New message". Your phone then fetches the encrypted message, decrypts it locally, and only then shows a preview. Push notifications are not enabled in current builds yet: they require an Apple developer account and will arrive with the App Store version. For now, messages arrive while the app is open.

heading: No telemetry
text: Sinhron does not phone home. The app sends no analytics, no usage statistics and no crash reports to the developers or to anyone else. Your phone only talks to the server you chose. If something goes wrong, any logs stay on your device, and it is up to you whether to share them in a bug report.

heading: Threat model
text: No messenger protects against everything. A threat model is an honest description of who might attack you, what Sinhron does about it, and where its protection ends. This page is a plain-language summary of the project's internal threat model.

heading: Why a threat model
text: Security claims are only useful if you know their limits. "End-to-end encrypted" says a lot about message content, but very little about metadata, a stolen phone or a compromised server. By writing down what we defend against and what we do not, we want to help you decide whether Sinhron fits your situation, and help reviewers hold us to our word. Sinhron is built for personal, family and team privacy. It is not designed to withstand a determined state-level adversary, and it has not yet been independently audited.

heading: What we protect against
text: Someone watching the network. Your internet provider, a public Wi-Fi operator or anyone in between sees only encrypted TLS connections. Inside them, messages are encrypted again with MLS. For extra protection, a server operator can pin their own certificate authority into the app, so that even a fraudulent certificate from a compromised public authority will not be accepted. A compromised or curious server. This is the central design goal. Even someone with full access to the server and its database dump gets only encrypted messages, encrypted attachments and an encrypted backup they cannot open. They cannot forge messages, because every message is signed by its sender and checked by the recipients. They cannot add themselves to a call, because call access is only granted to members of the chat. Push notification providers. Apple and Google deliver notifications, so they never receive message text, sender names or chat identifiers. A notification carries only your unread count. A malicious or removed group member. Only current members of a chat can read it. When someone is removed, the keys change and they cannot read anything sent afterwards. Thanks to forward secrecy, a key leake

heading: What's out of scope
text: Some threats are beyond what any app can solve, or beyond what Sinhron currently aims for: State-level adversaries who can compel server operators, observe networks at scale, or buy zero-day exploits. A compromised device. If your phone's operating system is compromised, or someone has physical access to it while it is unlocked, they can see what you see. The people you talk to. A chat partner can always take a screenshot, photograph the screen or forward what you wrote. Encryption cannot stop that, and neither can disappearing messages. Social engineering. If someone tricks you into revealing your 24-word key, they can take over your account. Network-level anonymity. Sinhron can hide your IP address from the server only through an optional SOCKS5 proxy such as Tor, which you install separately, and calls do not use it. Hiding the fact that you use Sinhron at all, or resisting large-scale traffic analysis, is a job for network tools like Tor. Root access to the server. An attacker who controls the server machine can disrupt service, tamper with the server software and see metadata. They still cannot read message content, but the operator is responsible for keeping the machine secur

heading: Known limitations today
text: We prefer to list these openly: No independent security audit yet. One is planned before a public launch. Metadata is visible to the server. The operator can see which accounts and devices are in which chats (it needs this to deliver ordinary messages and to admit people to calls), when messages are sent and delivered, approximately how big they are, and each chat's disappearing-messages timer. See What the server sees. Sealed sender still leaves traces. Most messages travel in a sealed envelope: the server does not learn which chat they belong to, and once the keys for anonymous sending have been shared, not which account sent them either. It still sees when each envelope arrives, whom it is for, and the timer attached to it. The first messages of a brand-new chat are sent with your account signed in until those keys have reached everyone. Your IP address is visible unless you use a proxy. An optional SOCKS5 proxy setting, for example Tor through the Orbot app, hides your IP address from the server. Without it the server sees your IP. Calls never go through the proxy, and the proxy has not yet been tried on a real iPhone. Size and timing patterns. Messages are padded to 512-byte b

heading: Reporting a vulnerability
text: If you find a security problem, we would be grateful to hear about it. Open an issue on GitHub, or contact the maintainers through their GitHub profiles. If the problem is serious and could put users at risk, please do not publish exploit details in a public issue. Open an issue asking for a private channel, or reach out to the maintainers directly through GitHub, and we will take it from there. Please include the version or commit you tested, steps to reproduce, and what you expected to happen. Thank you for helping keep Sinhron and its users safe.

heading: Running a server
text: Sinhron is designed to run on a server you control. This guide takes you from a fresh virtual machine to a working Sinhron server with encrypted messaging and calls. It assumes you are comfortable with SSH, a Linux firewall, Docker Compose and DNS records. The server works and is covered by tests, but Sinhron is in early beta and has not been independently audited. Calls across different networks on a real deployed server have not been fully tested yet. Run it for yourself, your family or a small team, and keep backups.

heading: What you'll need
text: Resource Minimum Recommended Typical cost --- --- --- --- Virtual machine 2 vCPU, 2 GB RAM, 20 GB SSD, Ubuntu 22.04 or newer 4 vCPU, 8 GB RAM, 50 GB SSD €5–30 per month (Hetzner), $15–120 per month (AWS, DigitalOcean) Domain name Any domain Whatever you like $10–30 per year Apple Developer account Optional, for push Needed for production iOS push $99 per year Apple push key (.p8) Optional Needed for production push Included with the developer account You will also need: Basic Linux skills: ssh, ufw, systemd. Basic Docker and Docker Compose. Access to your domain's DNS settings. Basic hygiene: SSH key login, fail2ban, a non-root user with sudo. A server on a VPS with its public IP directly on the network interface is the simplest option for calls (more on that below).

heading: Preparing the server
text: Log in, update the system, create a user and open only the ports Sinhron needs: Ports published by Docker (80, 443, 7881, 7882) bypass ufw, because Docker writes its own firewall rules. coturn runs on the host network, so ufw does apply to it. If your provider has an external firewall or security group, open the same list there too. Then disable root and password logins in /etc/ssh/sshdconfig (PermitRootLogin no, PasswordAuthentication no), reload SSH, and install Docker:

heading: DNS
text: Sinhron uses three host names, all pointing at your server's IP: Wait a few minutes, then check each name, for example dig turn.sinhron.example.com +short. Write down the public IP: it becomes TURNEXTERNALIP. If the IP is not on the VM's network interface (for example with 1:1 NAT on some clouds, where ip -4 addr does not show it), use the form public/private.

heading: Installation
text: Clone the repository: Everything the server needs lives in server/: Dockerfile, docker-compose.yml, Caddyfile and Dockerfile.caddy, livekit.yaml, turnserver.conf, the database migrations, and .env.example. Create your configuration from the template and make it readable only by you: The key settings, with placeholders to replace: Generate secrets like this: Messages are kept on the server, encrypted, for SINHRONMESSAGERETENTIONDAYS (14 by default) so that devices that were offline can catch up. .env.example also lists connection pool and rate-limit settings (SINHRONPG, SINHRONRATE); at the moment docker-compose.yml does not pass these to the container, so the server uses its built-in defaults. Now build and start everything: Next to docker-compose.yml there is a docker-compose.override.yml for local development. It exposes internal ports, turns off Caddy and changes how coturn is networked. A plain docker compose up picks it up automatically. In production, always run docker compose -f docker-compose.yml .... The compose file also takes care of a few safety details: Postgres listens only on 127.0.0.1, the server's port 8080 is reachable only through Caddy, and compose refuses to st

heading: TLS and domain
text: Sinhron uses Caddy as its front door. Caddy gets and renews TLS certificates from Let's Encrypt automatically for all three host names; you do not need to manage certificates yourself. The Caddyfile in the repository is used as is. Caddy is built from server/Dockerfile.caddy with the caddy-l4 module, which lets one port do two jobs. Connections to TCP 443 are routed by host name: The TURN name goes to coturn, with Caddy handling TLS. This lets calls work on networks that only allow HTTPS. Everything else goes to Caddy's normal web side: the API name serves /v1/ and the health checks, and the LiveKit name serves call signalling over secure WebSockets. Port 80 redirects to HTTPS and is used for Let's Encrypt validation. To receive certificate expiry notices, add email you@example.com to the global block of the Caddyfile. If you want maximum protection against a compromised public certificate authority, you can run your own CA and pin it into the client app at build time. No server changes are needed for that.

heading: Calls: LiveKit and coturn
text: Calls use two extra services, both started by the same compose file: LiveKit is the media server. It forwards encrypted audio and video between participants. Its signalling is reachable only through Caddy at wss:// on your LiveKit host name; media uses 7881/tcp and 7882/udp. coturn is a TURN/STUN relay that helps calls get through NAT and firewalls. It runs on the host network with relay ports 49152–49999/udp, and is also reachable as TURN over TLS on port 443. The Sinhron server issues short-lived LiveKit tickets and TURN credentials to app users. A LiveKit ticket is only issued to members of the chat. TURN logins do not contain user identities, so coturn's logs do not reveal who is calling. Credentials last TURNTTLSECS (24 hours by default), which is also the maximum length of a call. Check that TURN over TLS works: You should see subject=CN=turn.sinhron.example.com. Check that TURN can allocate a relay over UDP and TCP: Before you rely on calls, make a real test call between two physical devices on different networks, for example a phone on mobile data and another on Wi-Fi, then repeat with one of them on a network where only port 443 is open. LiveKit and coturn do not need an A

heading: Backups
text: The server never holds anything it can decrypt, so backups contain only encrypted data. You need three things: The Postgres database: accounts, groups, encrypted messages, encrypted user backups and attachment metadata. The media volume sinhronmedia: encrypted attachment files. Back it up at the same time as the database, because the two refer to each other. Your .env file, encrypted. A daily schedule with crontab -e might look like this: The repository also ships server/scripts/backup.sh, which does all three in one go: a Postgres dump, a media archive and a GPG-encrypted copy of .env (the passphrase is read from the file named in SINHRONBACKUPPASSFILE), keeping the last 14 days. To do it by hand, encrypt .env and keep the copy off the server: To restore on a new machine, start only Postgres, load the dump, then start the server. It applies migrations on top of the restored data automatically: Active connections and invitations that were still waiting for offline users are not part of the backup. Apps reconnect on their own.

heading: Updating
text: Database migrations run automatically when the server starts. Postgres and Caddy keep running, and apps reconnect by themselves after a short pause.

heading: Inviting people
text: Once your server is up, inviting people is simple: Ask them to install the Sinhron app. On the Pick a server screen, they enter your address, for example sinhron.example.com. They create a profile and write down their own 24-word key. To start chatting, you scan each other's QR code, or one of you pastes the other's key in New chat. The app has a field for an invite token, but the server does not require one yet. Anyone who knows your server's address can create an account. Registration is rate-limited, but invite-only registration is not available yet. Keep that in mind before sharing the address widely. Before going live, run through this checklist: SSH with keys only, firewall enabled, a long database password, .env with chmod 600, daily backups stored off the server, a Caddy email for certificate notices, fail2ban and automatic OS updates, and an uptime monitor. For what the server can and cannot see about your users, read Security and Threat model.

heading: Architecture
text: This page describes how Sinhron is put together: the app on your device, the services on the server, and the path a message or a call takes between them. It is written for curious users, self-hosters and contributors.

heading: The big picture
text: Sinhron has two halves. On your device, a Flutter interface sits on top of a Rust core that does all of the cryptography, storage and networking. On the server, Caddy terminates TLS and routes traffic to three services: the Sinhron server for messages, LiveKit for call media, and coturn for getting calls through firewalls. Everything is started with Docker Compose on a single machine. A Sinhron server is its own island: there is no federation between servers.

heading: The client: Flutter and Rust
text: The app is split into two layers with a strict boundary between them. Flutter draws the interface. Sinhron uses its own design system rather than stock Material or Cupertino widgets, so one codebase can look and feel polished on iOS, Android, macOS, Windows and Linux. Flutter handles screens, navigation, animations and state, and nothing else. The Rust core does everything sensitive: Cryptography: MLS group encryption (through OpenMLS), SFrame call keys, the 24-word BIP-39 key and the keys derived from it, attachment encryption. Storage: a local database encrypted with SQLCipher. Networking: the WebSocket connection, HTTPS requests, optional certificate pinning and an optional SOCKS5 proxy (for example Tor), all over rustls. Sync: applying incoming messages in order, removing duplicates and catching up after being offline. The two layers talk through flutterrustbridge, which generates the bindings automatically. Private keys are created and used only in Rust. The Flutter side gets what the screen needs to show; beyond that, it only passes the device key to the iOS Keychain for safekeeping and hands call keys to the call library, in memory. Decrypted photos and videos are kept in me

heading: The server
text: The server is deliberately simple, and deliberately not trusted with secrets. sinhron-server is written in Rust with Axum and Tokio. It registers accounts and their devices by public key (no passwords: devices prove who they are by signing a random challenge), stores KeyPackages, passes the sealed bundle when a new device is linked by QR code, delivers encrypted messages over WebSockets, keeps each user's encrypted backup, stores encrypted attachments, relays call signalling, and issues call tickets and TURN credentials. It also applies rate limits and deletes old data on schedule. PostgreSQL 16 stores accounts and their devices, group membership needed for delivery, and encrypted messages and sealed envelopes. Messages are kept for 14 days by default so offline devices can catch up. Blob storage is a Docker volume holding encrypted attachments, each named by the SHA-256 hash of its encrypted contents. Attachments are removed after 90 days without access. Caddy handles TLS certificates automatically and routes port 443 by host name. LiveKit forwards encrypted call media. coturn relays call traffic when devices cannot reach each other directly. The server never sees plain text. For

heading: How a message travels
text: Here is what happens when you send a message: You tap Send. The Flutter interface hands the text to the Rust core. The core packs it. The message is wrapped in a small typed envelope (so it can carry replies, reactions, edits, attachments or timers) and padded to a multiple of 512 bytes. The core encrypts and signs it as an MLS message for the chat's group, using the group's current keys. The core seals it. When the recipients have published their delivery keys, the core puts the MLS message into a separate sealed envelope (HPKE) for each recipient, so the server cannot tell which chat it belongs to. Otherwise the message is sent as it is. The app sends it with a unique message ID. If the app holds the access keys of everyone in the chat, sealed envelopes go over HTTPS without signing in to your account; otherwise they go over the secure WebSocket of your signed-in session. If you use a proxy, both go through it. The server stores the ciphertext and confirms receipt. You see the first tick. A sealed envelope is stored only for its recipient, with no link to the chat. The server delivers it to every device of every recipient that is online, including your own other devices if you ha

heading: How a call works
text: Ringing. When you start a call, the invitation travels through the Sinhron server over the existing WebSocket. If nobody answers within 30 seconds, the call ends. Tickets. Each device asks the Sinhron server for a LiveKit ticket and temporary TURN credentials. Tickets are only given to members of the chat. Keys. Each device derives SFrame keys from the chat's MLS group, as RFC 9605 describes. The keys are created locally and never leave the device. Connecting. The devices connect to LiveKit through Caddy. Media flows over WebRTC, either directly to LiveKit or through coturn. Coturn can relay over UDP, TCP or TLS on port 443 for networks that block everything else. Encrypting. Every audio and video frame is encrypted with SFrame before it leaves the device. LiveKit forwards frames it cannot decrypt. Rotating. If the chat's MLS keys change during the call, the call keys change with them. Recovering. If the network drops, the app gives the connection 30 seconds to recover before ending the call. Calls work in one-on-one chats and in groups. A group call is possible in chats of up to 32 people: everyone else in the chat is invited, people can join late, and the call goes on until only

heading: Standards
text: Sinhron relies on published standards rather than custom cryptography: RFC 9420: The Messaging Layer Security (MLS) Protocol. End-to-end encryption for one-on-one and group chats, with forward secrecy and post-compromise security. RFC 9605: Secure Frame (SFrame). End-to-end encryption of audio and video frames in calls, with keys derived from MLS. BIP-39: Mnemonic code for generating deterministic keys. The 24-word key that your account is derived from. RFC 9180: Hybrid Public Key Encryption (HPKE). Used inside MLS, for the sealed sender envelopes that hide which chat a message belongs to, and for handing keys to a new device linked by QR code. You can also browse these on the IETF Datatracker.

heading: Roadmap
text: This page shows where Sinhron stands today and what comes next. It reflects the project's internal status tracking. We do not give dates: things ship when they are ready and tested.

heading: Where we are
text: Sinhron is in early beta. The core is in place: end-to-end encrypted chats and groups, a working server, encrypted storage and backup, calls, several devices per account, sealed sender, and a polished messaging experience. The project's technical plan is divided into ten phases, from the first scaffolding to a security audit and store distribution. About eight of them are covered in code. Much of it still needs testing on real phones. What is still missing before a public release is mostly about trust and reach: testing on real devices, an independent security audit, signed builds and distribution.

heading: Done
text: Encryption and accounts End-to-end encrypted one-on-one and group chats using MLS (RFC 9420). Accounts without email, phone number or password, based on a 24-word BIP-39 key. Encrypted backup of your chat membership on the server, restorable with your 24 words. Fully encrypted local database (SQLCipher). Message padding to hide exact lengths, and push notification payloads without content. Safety numbers (60 digits or QR code, scannable with the camera) with warnings when a contact's key changes, including for each member of a group. Sealed sender: the server sees neither which chat a message belongs to nor which account sent it. An optional SOCKS5 / Tor proxy also hides your IP address. Several devices per account: link a new device by scanning a QR code; each device has its own key, and removing a device locks it out. Your main identity key stays on your first device only. Server Rust server with WebSocket delivery, offline catch-up, rate limiting and automatic cleanup. Docker Compose deployment with automatic TLS (Caddy and Let's Encrypt). Encrypted attachment storage. Old messages are removed a whole month at a time. Automated tests for the server, the encryption core and the a

heading: In progress
text: Photos, video, files and voice messages. Implemented and tested in code, including albums, a gallery, recording video with the camera, voice messages with hands-free recording, and optional link previews. Video gets a preview frame and is compressed before sending. Still to do: verification on real devices. Calls across networks on a real server. The setup for getting calls through NAT and firewalls is in place, but a full acceptance test on a deployed server with devices on different networks is still pending. Testing on two real phones. Several devices per account, group calls and blocking are built and tested in code, but haven't yet been tried on real iPhones. Push notifications and incoming calls when the app is closed. The server side is ready. The app side needs an Apple developer certificate, which has not been set up yet.

heading: Next
text: First releases on GitHub Releases. Security audit preparation, followed by an independent audit. Reproducible builds, so anyone can check that a published app matches the source code. Code signing and distribution: App Store, Google Play, F-Droid and desktop packages. Builds for more platforms. Development currently focuses on iPhone; the Flutter codebase targets Android, macOS, Windows and Linux too.

heading: Not planned for 1.0
text: Some things are deliberately left out of the first version: A web client. Browsers make secure key storage and supply-chain safety much harder. It remains an open question for later. Federation. Each Sinhron server is its own island. Servers do not talk to each other, and there are no bridges to other networks. Post-quantum encryption. Planned once the MLS library we use supports it, without breaking existing chats. Encrypted backup of message history. Version 1.0 backs up your chat membership, not your messages. Cloud AI features such as translation or summaries. They conflict with keeping your data private. Call recording. Server-side search. This will never be built: search always runs on your device.

heading: FAQ
text: Short answers to the questions people ask most often. If yours is not here, feel free to open an issue on GitHub.

heading: How is Sinhron different from Signal and Telegram?
text: Compared with Telegram: in Telegram, regular chats and groups are encrypted between you and Telegram's servers, but not end to end, so the service can technically read them. End-to-end encryption is only available in one-on-one secret chats. In Sinhron, everything is end-to-end encrypted, always: every chat, every group, every call. There is no other mode. Compared with Signal: Signal is an excellent, well-audited end-to-end encrypted messenger. The main differences are where it runs and how you sign up. Signal runs on servers operated by the Signal Foundation and asks for a phone number. Sinhron runs on a server you or someone you trust operates, and asks for no phone number, email or password: your account is a 24-word key. Sinhron also uses MLS (RFC 9420), the newer IETF standard for group encryption. The trade-off: Signal and Telegram are mature, widely used and, in Signal's case, independently audited. Sinhron is in early beta and has not been audited yet.

heading: Do I need my own server?
text: No. You need access to a Sinhron server, which can be run by you, your family, your company or a friend you trust. If someone you know already runs one, you just enter its address when you first open the app. If you would like to run your own, see Self-hosting. A small virtual machine and a domain name are enough.

heading: Why a server if you can't trust it?
text: Phones are often offline, behind firewalls, or asleep. Something has to hold messages until the recipient comes back online, help devices find each other, and relay calls. That is the server's job. Sinhron is designed so that the server can do this job without being able to read anything. It only ever handles encrypted data. Even someone with full access to the server and its database cannot read your messages, see your photos or listen to your calls. They can still see some metadata, such as who talks to whom and when. That is one more reason to choose a server operator you trust. Details are in Security.

heading: What if I lose my 24-word key?
text: As long as you still have your phone, nothing changes: Sinhron keeps working. But if you then lose or reset your phone, your account cannot be recovered. The 24 words are the only way to open your encrypted backup, and they are never sent to the server. Nobody can reset them: not us, and not your server's operator. In that case you would need to create a new account and reconnect with your contacts. This is why the app asks you to write the words on paper and checks three of them before you finish setting up.

heading: Is there a web version?
text: No. A web client is not planned for version 1.0. Browsers make it much harder to store keys securely and to guarantee that the code you run has not been tampered with. Sinhron is a native app for phones and computers.

heading: Can I use it on several devices?
text: Yes, in beta. The new device shows a QR code, and you scan it with the device where you created your account; on any other device of yours, that step asks for your 24 words. You can also simply type your 24 words on the new device. Each device gets its own key rather than sharing one private key, and your main identity key stays on your first device only. Once linked, the new device receives the recent messages of each chat (up to 200) from one of your other devices. You can remove a device in the Devices list, and the server stops letting it in. This has not yet been tested on two real iPhones.

heading: How many people can a server handle?
text: Sinhron is designed for up to about 10,000 active users per server. A small virtual machine is plenty for a family or a small team. Groups are designed for up to 100 members at first.

heading: Is it free?
text: Sinhron is open source, and there is no paid Sinhron service. The only cost is running a server: a small virtual machine and a domain name, if you host your own. The license has not been finalised yet.

heading: Has it been audited?
text: Not yet. Sinhron uses open, well-studied standards (MLS, SFrame, BIP-39) and established open-source libraries, and the project keeps an internal threat model. But no independent security audit has been done. An audit is planned before a public release. Until then, please do not rely on Sinhron for situations where your safety depends on it.

heading: How can I help?
text: Thank you for asking. A few ways: Try it and report problems. Open an issue on GitHub with steps to reproduce. Review the code, especially the cryptography and the server. Security reports are very welcome; see Reporting a vulnerability. Run a test server and tell us how the Self-hosting guide worked for you. Improve the documentation if something here is unclear.

heading: Glossary
text: Sinhron uses a handful of technical terms. Here they are in plain language, roughly in the order you are likely to meet them.

heading: End-to-end encryption (E2EE)
text: Encryption where a message is locked on the sender's device and can only be unlocked on the recipients' devices. Servers and networks in between only ever see scrambled data. In Sinhron, end-to-end encryption is always on.

heading: MLS
text: Messaging Layer Security, an open IETF standard for end-to-end encrypted group messaging, published as RFC 9420. Sinhron uses it for every chat, including one-on-one chats, through the OpenMLS library.

heading: Group and epoch
text: In MLS, every chat is a group: the set of devices that share its keys. Each time the group's keys change, for example when someone joins or leaves or keys are refreshed, the group moves to a new epoch. Messages from one epoch cannot be read with another epoch's keys.

heading: KeyPackage
text: A small bundle of public key material that a device publishes on the server in advance. It lets others add you to a chat even while you are offline, without a back-and-forth exchange.

heading: Forward secrecy
text: A property that keeps past messages safe even if a key is stolen later. Because keys keep changing, today's key cannot unlock yesterday's messages.

heading: Post-compromise security
text: The mirror image of forward secrecy: if a device's keys were compromised, the group recovers once keys are refreshed, and the attacker is locked out of future messages.

heading: SFrame
text: Secure Frame, a standard for end-to-end encrypting audio and video frames in calls, published as RFC 9605. Sinhron derives SFrame keys from the chat's MLS keys, so only chat members can see or hear a call.

heading: SFU
text: Selective Forwarding Unit: a media server that receives each participant's audio and video and forwards it to the others without mixing it. With SFrame on top, an SFU forwards encrypted frames it cannot decrypt.

heading: LiveKit
text: The open-source SFU that Sinhron uses for calls. It runs on the same server as Sinhron and only ever handles encrypted media.

heading: TURN/STUN (coturn)
text: Helpers for connecting calls across home routers, firewalls and mobile networks. STUN helps a device find its public address; TURN relays traffic when a direct path is not possible. Sinhron uses coturn, an open-source TURN/STUN server, which can also relay over port 443 for networks that only allow HTTPS.

heading: Sealed sender
text: A technique that hides who sent a message from the server, which then only knows who should receive it. In Sinhron, each recipient gets the message in its own sealed envelope (HPKE, RFC 9180), so the server does not learn which chat it belongs to. Once access keys have been shared inside the chat, envelopes are sent without signing in, so the server does not learn which account sent them either. The first messages of a new chat are still sent signed in. Your IP address can be hidden too, with the optional Tor proxy.

heading: BIP-39 and the 24-word key
text: BIP-39 is a widely used standard for turning a random secret into a list of words that people can write down. Sinhron generates 24 words for your account. All of your keys are derived from them, and they are the only way to restore your account.

heading: Safety number
text: A 60-digit number (12 groups of 5) computed from your key and your contact's key. It is the same on both phones. Comparing it, in person or by scanning a QR code, proves that nobody is intercepting your conversation.

heading: SQLCipher
text: An encrypted version of SQLite, the database that many apps use to store data on the device. Sinhron uses it so that your chats are encrypted on your device as well as in transit.

heading: Self-hosting
text: Running a service on a server you or someone you trust controls, rather than relying on a company's central servers. Sinhron is designed to be self-hosted with Docker Compose.

heading: Metadata
text: Information about communication rather than its content: who talks to whom, when, how often and how much. End-to-end encryption hides content, but a server still sees some metadata. Sinhron works to minimise it and documents what remains in Security.
